reviews.feedback:
Eval 0 with_skill: confirmed pass on substance. RAG-over-FT gives 5 real reasons
(wrong gap, invents clause text, retrain cadence, no labels, still need RAG). The
actual skill-vs-baseline separation this run was assertion 2 (managed-vs-self-host
matrix), NOT the tagged discriminator (assertion 1) — baseline also passed RAG-with-reason.

Grader: assertion 2 matched on "managed" in the short answer, not the §4 trade-off
table. Tighten so "managed RAG" alone fails — require SageMaker/self-host or
instance-hour-vs-per-token in the evidence.

Skill: keep this shape. The discriminator to harden for iteration 2 is
managed-vs-self-host (the only real miss on baseline); RAG-with-reason is necessary
but no longer sufficient to isolate skill value here.

Eval 0 without_skill (baseline): 3/4, correctly graded. Fails assertion 2 —
frames Q Business vs Bedrock KB (both managed), no SageMaker/self-host tier.

IMPORTANT — where baseline beat the skill: it introduced Amazon Q Business,
which is arguably the BEST fit for "internal employee portal over 4,000 policy
PDFs" (purpose-built, permission-aware, ready UI, per-user pricing). The
with-skill answer never mentioned it. The skill's service-selection spectrum
(Bedrock KB / SageMaker / AgentCore) has a gap exactly where this prompt's
best answer lives — the purpose-built managed assistant tier (Q Business).
Iteration 2 should add Q Business to the assess matrix or the managed-service
branch.

Baseline also sharper on: Provisioned Throughput as a named cost trap (skill
buried it in a levers list); concrete cost numbers and a pilot plan (skill
ended on a confirm-list).

Baseline weaker (skill's real edge): hard-codes "Claude 3.5 Haiku/Sonnet" as
permanent — the exact deprecation antipattern the skill corrects; no
managed-vs-self-host spectrum; no separate-axis human gate; no risk handoff.

Net: the +25 on assertion 2 is real, but the skill's matrix is missing a row.
The baseline found the better default service for this specific prompt.

Eval 1 with_skill: 4/4 confirmed, all genuine. Distinctly better-grounded than
baseline despite Δ0 — the depth is corpus-driven, not general knowledge.

Highest-value contribution: the Cedar/tool-boundary separation ("guardrails
never see a tool call"). A generic answer puts guardrails on input+output and
stops; this answer names the structural gap and fills it with Cedar permit/deny
before write tools. That's the skill encoding a trap, not restating knowledge.

Other non-obvious depth the baseline likely lacked: use_aws tool rejection,
aws:sourceVpce enforcement (private-capable vs private-enforced), HYBRID search
for policy-number exact tokens, Lambda ops notes (init outside handler,
PackageType: Image, 15-min ceiling as single-agent argument), memory silent-gap
warning. Corpus citations throughout (ch04/ch06/ch07/ch08).

Nits: (1) hard-codes titan-embed/cohere IDs while saying "never hard-code" —
defensible as re-verify markers in a design doc, but note the tension. (2) Cedar
recommendation leads with AgentCore Policy, then admits the host is Lambda and
offers Verified Permissions as the equivalent — consider leading with the
Lambda-applicable path. (3) Large surface area (Strands/AgentCore/Cedar/A2A/
Gateway) for a user who asked four focused questions — faithful to the skill
but dense.

Eval weakness (agree with rubric): tests tasks Opus already aces. The two-ARN
discriminator passed on both configs. Iteration 2 should add a harder discriminator
— e.g. the Cedar/tool-boundary gap, or the region-wildcard failover detail —
something the baseline wouldn't produce from general knowledge.

Eval 1 without_skill (baseline): 4/4, correctly graded. All four assertions pass
on substance — the two-ARN trap is named correctly with the region-wildcard
detail, guardrails placed at model invocation, vector-store trade-off concrete,
single-agent reasoning honest. The Δ0 is real on the assertions.

Where baseline beat the skill: digestibility (~7k vs ~22.7k tokens), concrete
5-step build order, IAM policy in one block, "console works but Lambda gets
AccessDenied" framing.

capture:
1. CEDAR/TOOL-BOUNDARY GAP (the big one): baseline says "guardrails enforced
   server-side, can't be bypassed" and stops. Never identifies that guardrails
   don't see tool calls. For an insurance assistant that can file claims, the

2. No trust-boundary split with separate read/write roles.
3. No PrivateLink / aws:sourceVpce enforcement.
4. No Lambda ops guidance (init outside handler, PackageType: Image, 15-min).
5. No HYBRID search for policy-number exact tokens.
6. No memory silent-gap warning.

CONFIRMS eval 1 is weak: the four assertions test things Opus already knows.
The skill's actual value (Cedar gap, trust split, PrivateLink, Lambda ops) is
not tested. Iteration 2 should add an assertion for the tool-boundary/guardrail
gap — that would turn Δ0 into a real +25, because the baseline misses it
entirely.

Eval 2 with_skill: 4/4 confirmed, all genuine. Correct, complete tool-use loop —
verbatim assistant echo, toolUseId echoed, tool results on user turn, content as
list of blocks, error handling with status:error, multiple tool calls per turn.

Legacy-format discriminator (assertion 2) satisfied by explicit warning, not
use — negation-aware grader correct. Baseline also passed it, so it didn't
discriminate this run.

client (offline-testable with Stubber — pre-wires eval 4's discriminator into

note, ThrottlingException vs AccessDeniedException distinction. The skill isn't
just writing a correct loop — it's writing one that's testable offline, deployable
without the AccessDenied trap, and resistant to the legacy bug.

Nits: (1) no max-iterations guard on the while True — a misbehaving model loops
forever. (2) MODEL_ID hard-coded in __main__ despite "never hard-code" rule —
defensible as example, note the tension. (3) temperature:0 not commented.

Eval weakness (agree with rubric): tests tasks Opus already aces. The skill's

for the injected-client/testability seam or the inference-profile warning —

3. No ARM64/Graviton, no DockerImageFunction variant, no corpus citation.

Eval 4 with_skill: 4/4 confirmed, all genuine. This is the skill's clearest win —
the discriminator (moto cannot mock bedrock-runtime) is the exact non-obvious
gotcha the skill encodes, and the baseline missed it entirely (benchmark.json:
"does not note moto's bedrock-runtime gap").

The skill makes the gap the structural foundation, not a footnote: "This is not
a preference — moto cannot mock bedrock-runtime at all, so Stubber is the only
pure-unit path." The whole strategy is organized around Stubber-for-runtime,
moto-for-infra, and here's why you can't swap them.

Distinctly skill-driven depth: dependency injection as the prerequisite (connects
to eval 2's injected client), assert_no_pending_responses as termination proof,
Stubber's contract-test property (catches API drift via service-model validation),
StreamingBody parse contract, error-path discipline (ThrottlingException retryable
vs AccessDenied not, branch on Error Code not message), three-layer CI isolation
(no creds + IMDS disabled + double latch), mypy with boto3-stubs, two-ARN IAM test
via moto (connects to eval 3), layered order cheapest-first.

Nits: (1) "I ran it just now — 7 passed" claim appears twice — verify the agent
actually executed the harness; if the eval runner doesn't execute code, this is
a hallucinated claim that misleads. (2) Repo file references
(.claude/skills/aws-ai-validate/scripts/tests/...) resolve in the skill's source
repo but may not exist in the user's workspace — a reader in a different repo
would find them missing.

This is the eval the rubric calls "a real, honest win" — confirmed. The +25 is
earned, not inflated.

Eval 4 without_skill (baseline): 3/4, correctly graded. Fails assertion 2 —
and the miss is subtle but real.

The baseline says "moto does not meaningfully emulate model inference: there's
no real LLM behind bedrock-runtime.converse." This sounds like it addresses the
gap but doesn't. The actual gotcha: moto cannot mock bedrock-runtime AT ALL —
the service client itself is not implemented, so you can't even stub a canned
response through it. The baseline's framing ("no LLM behind it") would lead a
developer to try moto first and get a confusing error. The with-skill answer
names the specific gap (API absent, not just model absent) and prevents the
detour. The +25 is earned.

Where baseline BEAT the skill: (1) pytest-socket --disable-socket as a
network-level guard ("a forgotten stub becomes a SocketBlockedError, not a
bill") — with-skill doesn't mention it. (2) converse_stream boundary-fake
pattern — with-skill mentions streaming but doesn't show how to test it.
(3) conftest.py autouse fixture is cleaner than with-skill's CI-specific YAML.
(4) No "I ran it" hallucination risk.

Where baseline is weaker: (1) the discriminator — misses the specific
bedrock-runtime gap. (2) No double latch for real-AWS smoke. (3) No reference
to existing repo harness. (4) No mypy/boto3-stubs. (5) No two-ARN IAM test via
moto. (6) Hard-codes bare model id (anthropic.claude-3-5-sonnet-...) without
us. prefix — inconsistent with deploy eval's lesson.

Iteration note: the skill should adopt pytest-socket and the converse_stream
boundary-fake pattern from the baseline — both are genuine improvements.

Eval 5 with_skill: 3/3 confirmed, all genuine. This is the skill's biggest and
most honest win — +67, the largest delta in the set, with both discriminators
(assertions 2 and 3) being the router's core contribution.

The five-stage pipeline (assess → design → build → deploy → validate) is
presented as a named, structured process with a "Touches AWS?" column that makes
the offline-first discipline visual. The Accidental Architecture antipattern
is named at the top as the thing the process exists to prevent. Stage 1 is
the answer to "where do I start" — a structured conversation, not code.

Offline-first is emphasized structurally, not as a footnote: the "Touches AWS?"
column (No/No/Not for real/No/Only here), the guardrails section ("No AWS calls
until you say go"), and the binding.toml mention ("AWS profile stays unset
until the gated Stage-5 step — by design").

Distinctly skill-driven depth: the six determinations of Stage 1 (embedded
aws-ai-assess methodology), the service spectrum trade-off matrix, the
customization ladder with knowledge-vs-behavior distinction, the fast-path
4-step decision tree, the antipatterns section (self-hosting RAG on SageMaker,
fine-tuning for low/spiky volume, hard-coding model IDs, jumping to Stage 3),
and the concrete next step (six questions to kick off Stage 1).

Nits: (1) very long for a "where do I start" question — but the user asked for
"the actual process/steps" so comprehensive is appropriate, and the fast-path
section helps. (2) binding.toml mention is inside-baseball for a first-time
user. (3) ends by asking the user to start Stage 1 immediately — right UX for
the router, but a user who just wanted "the steps" might not expect to start
working through them.

This is the eval the rubric calls "the router's core value and where the skill
most outperforms a generic answer" — confirmed. The +67 is earned. The
baseline's 33% (passed only "starts with the use case") proves the router's
contribution is real, not inflated.

Eval 5 without_skill (baseline): 1/3, correctly graded. Passes assertion 1
(starts with the use case). Fails both discriminators: no five-stage pipeline
(7-step generic process), no offline-first discipline (encourages console
access in Step 3).

The +67 is earned — both misses are the router's core contribution.

Where baseline is genuinely BETTER than the skill: (1) Step 0's three questions
are sharper and more digestible than the skill's six determinations — "what's
the cost of being wrong?" is a framing the skill doesn't use. (2) Step 3
(prototype cheaply with the playground) is practical for a beginner — the skill
never mentions the playground. (3) Step 6 gives concrete eval practices (test
set, score outputs, track cost/latency) the skill doesn't. (4) Step 7 gives
monitoring practices (CloudWatch, model invocation logging, budget alerts, %
rollout) the skill doesn't. (5) Mentions Amazon Q — same gap as eval 0. (6)
More compact and actionable.

HONEST TRADE-OFF: the skill is more disciplined (named pipeline, offline-first,
credential-gated, antipattern-aware) — right for production/CI. The baseline is
more practical for a first prototype (playground, real cheap calls, iterate fast)
— right for a beginner exploring. The eval rewards the discipline, but a real
user who's never touched Bedrock might prefer the baseline's approach.

Iteration-2 suggestion for the skill: acknowledge the playground-prototype path
as a legitimate early exploration step (with a caveat that it's manual, not
CI-automated), rather than treating ALL real-AWS access as gated to Stage 5.
